explanation.correct: Dimension tables provide the descriptive attributes used to filter, group, and label fact table data — examples: Date (year, month, day, quarter), Customer (name, region, segment), Product (category, brand, SKU).
explanation.incorrect: Dimension tables provide analytical context for facts — any descriptive attribute, not just physical dimensions or dates.
explanation.examTip: Common dimension tables: Date (always have one!), Customer, Product, Geography, Employee, Channel. Date dimension is critical — pre-populated with every date and attributes like IsWeekend, Quarter, Holiday.

questions.scenarioText: A company stores customer purchase data in a data warehouse used by marketing, finance, and operations. Each department has defined their customer ID field differently: marketing uses email, finance uses account number, operations uses phone number.
questions.questionText: What governance solution addresses this root problem?

options.text: Build separate data warehouses for each department
Implement a data dictionary and MDM program to establish a canonical customer identifier used consistently across all systems
Use ETL to convert all customer IDs to email addresses before loading
Train each department to use their own definition and accept the inconsistency

explanation.correct: This is a classic MDM problem — inconsistent entity definitions across systems. The solution is a data dictionary defining the canonical customer identifier and an MDM program creating a golden customer record that all systems reference.
explanation.incorrect: Separate DWs multiply the inconsistency. Forcing one format (email) as ID may not be unique or available. Accepting inconsistency = broken analytics.
explanation.examTip: When different systems use different IDs for the same entity = MDM problem. Golden record = authoritative source everyone uses. Data dictionary = ensures consistent definitions.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a sample and a population in statistics?

options.text: A sample is always larger than the population
A population is the complete set of all relevant items; a sample is a subset selected from the population
A population is studied using surveys; a sample uses databases
They are interchangeable terms in data analytics

explanation.correct: Population = every member of the group being studied (all customers, all transactions). Sample = a subset of the population. We use samples when analysing the full population is impractical.
explanation.incorrect: Samples are always smaller than or equal to the population. The distinction isn't about data collection method or interchangeable.
explanation.examTip: Population = census (complete). Sample = subset. Statistical inference uses sample data to draw conclusions about the population. Larger, random samples = more reliable conclusions.

questions.questionText: Match each scenario to the BEST chart type.

dropdowns.prompt: Show what percentage each product category contributes to total revenue
Show the frequency distribution of customer ages
Show whether advertising spend correlates with sales revenue

explanation.correct: Part-to-whole = pie chart (ideal for ≤6 categories). Distribution of continuous variable = histogram. Relationship between two continuous variables = scatter plot.
explanation.incorrect: Each chart type serves a specific data relationship. Mismatching chart to data type obscures the insight.
explanation.examTip: Chart selection cheat sheet: Comparison → bar. Trend over time → line. Part-to-whole → pie/stacked. Distribution → histogram/box. Relationship → scatter. Hierarchy → treemap.

questions.questionText: What is imputation in data preparation?

options.text: Removing rows with missing values from the dataset
Filling in missing values with estimated or calculated replacement values
Importing data from external sources to supplement the dataset
Computing aggregate values to add new derived columns

explanation.correct: Imputation replaces missing (NULL) values with substitutes — mean imputation (replace with column mean), median imputation, mode imputation, forward/backward fill (for time series), or ML-based prediction.
explanation.incorrect: Imputation fills missing values — it's not deletion, import, or aggregation.
explanation.examTip: Imputation methods: Mean (risk: reduces variance), Median (better for skewed data), Mode (categorical), KNN imputation (uses similar records), Multiple imputation (creates multiple versions for uncertainty). Choose based on data type and missingness pattern.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a data audit?

options.text: Auditing the performance of data analysts
A systematic examination of data systems, processes, and quality to ensure compliance with policies and standards
Calculating the financial cost of all company data
Auditing database query logs for performance optimisation

explanation.correct: A data audit examines data processes, quality, governance controls, and compliance — identifying gaps in data quality, access control violations, policy non-compliance, or risk areas.
explanation.incorrect: Data audits are compliance and governance checks, not performance reviews, financial calculations, or query optimisation.
explanation.examTip: Data audit types: quality audit (is data accurate?), access audit (who accessed what?), compliance audit (are we following regulations?), process audit (are ETL processes working correctly?).

questions.questionText: What is a KPI threshold or target?

options.text: A legal limit on how much data can be stored
A predefined value that a KPI is measured against to determine if performance is on track, at risk, or failing
The maximum threshold for data storage costs
A filter applied to a KPI to remove outliers from the calculation

explanation.correct: KPI targets define success — e.g., Customer Satisfaction > 85% (green), 75-85% (yellow/at risk), < 75% (red/failing). Thresholds enable traffic-light dashboards and automated alerts.
explanation.incorrect: KPI thresholds are performance benchmarks, not legal limits, storage costs, or data filters.
explanation.examTip: Dashboard traffic lights: green (meeting target), yellow (approaching risk threshold), red (failing). Define targets during requirements gathering, not after seeing the data.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between discrete and continuous data?

options.text: Discrete is digital; continuous is analogue
Discrete data can only take specific, countable values; continuous data can take any value within a range
Continuous data requires a database; discrete data can only be stored in spreadsheets
Discrete data is collected continuously over time; continuous data is collected at intervals

explanation.correct: Discrete: specific countable values with no values in between (number of employees: 5, 10, 15 — never 5.3). Continuous: any value within a range (height: 5.67ft, temperature: 98.6°F).
explanation.incorrect: Discrete vs continuous is about possible values, not storage medium, collection frequency, or digital/analogue.
explanation.examTip: Discrete examples: number of orders, number of defects, employee headcount. Continuous examples: weight, height, temperature, time, revenue. Key: can you have a fractional value?

questions.questionText: What is a calculated field in a BI tool or spreadsheet?

options.text: A field that is calculated by the database before it is returned in a query
A new column or measure derived from existing data using a formula or expression
A field that calculates how much data storage is being used
A numeric field that has been validated against a calculation rule

explanation.correct: Calculated fields create new measures or dimensions from existing data — e.g., Profit = Revenue - Cost, Profit_Margin = Profit / Revenue * 100, Age = DATEDIFF(BirthDate, TODAY()).
explanation.incorrect: Calculated fields are user-defined derived metrics, not database computations, storage metrics, or validation rules.
explanation.examTip: Calculated fields in Tableau: drag to columns/rows to use as if they were real data. In Power BI: DAX measures (dynamic aggregations) vs calculated columns (row-by-row). Know the difference.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of conditional formatting in data visualisation?

options.text: Formatting that only applies when data analysis conditions are met
Automatically changing the appearance of cells or data points based on their values to highlight patterns
A conditional branch in the data pipeline that changes format based on data type
Formatting applied only when a user has conditional access permissions

explanation.correct: Conditional formatting automatically highlights data based on rules — red for values below target, green for above; heat map colour scales; data bars; icon sets — enabling pattern recognition at a glance.
explanation.incorrect: Conditional formatting is a visualisation technique for dynamic highlighting, not pipeline logic, access control, or analysis prerequisites.
explanation.examTip: Excel conditional formatting: colour scales (gradient), data bars, icon sets (arrows/traffic lights), highlight cell rules. Power BI/Tableau: background colour rules, font colour by value.

questions.questionText: What does GDPR stand for and who does it apply to?

options.text: General Data Privacy Regulation — applies only to EU government agencies
General Data Protection Regulation — applies to any organisation processing personal data of EU residents, regardless of where the organisation is located
Global Data Protection Rules — applies only to multinational companies with revenue over €50 million
General Data Processing Requirements — a voluntary certification for EU-based companies

explanation.correct: GDPR (2018) is the EU's data protection regulation. It has extraterritorial reach — any organisation anywhere in the world that processes personal data of EU residents must comply. Fines up to 4% of global annual revenue.
explanation.incorrect: GDPR applies broadly to any processor of EU residents' data, not just government, large companies, or EU-based organisations.
explanation.examTip: GDPR key rights: access, rectification, erasure (right to be forgotten), portability, objection, restriction. Key obligations: lawful basis, consent, privacy by design, breach notification (72 hours).

questions.questionText: What is year-over-year (YoY) analysis?

options.text: Comparing data from the current month to the same month last year
Comparing data from the current period (year, quarter, month) to the same period in the prior year to measure growth or decline
Analysing data collected over multiple years in a single view
A forecast that spans one full year

explanation.correct: YoY compares the same time period across consecutive years — Q2 2024 vs Q2 2023, January 2024 vs January 2023 — removing seasonal effects to show true growth or decline.
explanation.incorrect: YoY is specifically about same-period comparison year-to-year, not just monthly, multi-year view, or forecasting.
explanation.examTip: YoY formula: (Current Period - Prior Year Same Period) / Prior Year Same Period × 100%. Better than comparing consecutive months which may have seasonal distortion.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it represents good data visualisation practice.

statements.text: A dashboard should show only the KPIs most relevant to the audience's decisions.
Using 3D charts always makes data easier to understand.
Including the data source and date on charts improves transparency and trust.
Using dual-axis charts always misleads the audience.

explanation.correct: Relevant KPIs only = focused, actionable. Source/date = transparency. 3D charts = distort proportions, harder to read (bad practice). Dual-axis charts = can be appropriate when clearly labelled (not always misleading).
explanation.incorrect: 3D charts almost always make interpretation harder. Dual-axis charts are useful when two metrics have different scales — just label them clearly.
explanation.examTip: Visualisation best practices: purpose-driven (what decision does this support?), minimal clutter, clear labels, appropriate chart type, start axes at zero for bar charts, include data source.

questions.scenarioText: A data analyst notices that revenue figures in the CRM system show $5.2M for Q3, but the finance system shows $4.9M for the same period. Both numbers are being reported to executives from different departments.
questions.questionText: What is the root cause of this problem and what governance solution addresses it?

options.text: Data accuracy error — fix the numbers in the CRM

Lack of a single source of truth and inconsistent metric definitions — implement data governance with a certified 'official' revenue metric and a data dictionary defining exactly how revenue is calculated
A timeliness issue — the data in one system hasn't been updated
A technical ETL bug — fix the pipeline extracting data from CRM to Finance

explanation.correct: This is a classic 'single source of truth' problem. CRM may count booked revenue; Finance may count recognised revenue — different definitions. Governance solution: data dictionary defining the official revenue metric, designating the authoritative source, and certifying metrics that appear in reports.
explanation.incorrect: Without knowing the definition difference, you can't say which is 'wrong'. It may not be a timeliness or ETL issue — it may be intentionally different metrics.
explanation.examTip: Single source of truth (SSOT) issues are common when multiple systems independently track the same metric. Solution: define metrics in a data dictionary, certify official versions, and govern which source is authoritative.
